 oracular vapour] S. draws in this scene on various classical and contemporary accounts of ora-
cles, particularly the oracle at Delphi; Panthea and, more importantly, Asia, are inspired to prophesy
in the manner of a priestess intoxicated by vapour from an oracular cavern. S.’s most direct sources
are Plutarch, Moralia, ‘De defectu oraculorum’, xl, xliii, l; Diodorus Siculus xvi 26; Lucan, Pharsalia v
82–101 and ix 564–5; and see also Barthelemy ii 391–2 and note xx. For analogues with Virgil’s account
of the Cumaean Sybil cp. Aeneid vi 240ff.; S. and Mary visited the landscape of Virgil’s poem during
their stay in Naples (see L ii 61). On S.’s conception of the vapour itself, see below, note to line 44.

Fit throne for such a Power! Magnificent!
 How glorious art thou, Earth! and if thou be
The shadow of some Spirit lovelier still,
Though evil stain its work, and it should be
15 Like its creation, weak yet beautiful,
I could fall down and worship that and thee —
Even now my heart adoreth — Wonderful!
 Look Sister — ere the vapour dim thy brain:
